## The pitch

Bioinformatics workflows boil down to a small set of motifs: load a matrix,
normalize it, look for structure, and call out the rows or columns that don't
behave like the rest. The same motifs work fine on baseball, and baseball has
the advantage of being immediately legible — you don't need to know what a
gene does to recognize a player having a hot month.

This notebook walks through four canonical visualisations against the 2026
Seattle Mariners, six weeks into the season:

| Bioinformatics view              | Baseball mapping                                |
|----------------------------------|-------------------------------------------------|
| count / expression matrix        | player × stat table                             |
| z-scored heatmap with clustering | offensive profile heatmap                       |
| volcano plot                     | observed wOBA vs Statcast xwOBA, sized by PA    |
| PCA on samples                   | player profile embedding, coloured by position  |

## Environment

Reproducibility is handled with [`renv`](https://rstudio.github.io/renv/).
Open the project in **Positron**, run `renv::restore()` once, and every
package version below is pinned to the lockfile checked into the repo.

```{r setup}
source(here::here("R", "00_setup.R"))
```

## 1 · Load the matrix

```{r fetch}
source(here::here("R", "01_fetch_data.R"))
batting  <- readRDS(here("data", "batting_2026.rds"))
pitching <- readRDS(here("data", "pitching_2026.rds"))

batting |> dplyr::arrange(dplyr::desc(pa)) |> head(8) |> knitr::kable(digits = 3)
```

The fetch step prefers the live MLB Stats API via `baseballr::mlb_team_stats()`.
When the call fails — offline laptop, rate limit, conference Wi-Fi — it falls
back to a deterministic synthetic dataset so the rest of the notebook
always renders. Same pattern you'd use to ship a teaching notebook that
doesn't need a live database connection.

## 2 · Heatmap

```{r heatmap, fig.width = 10, fig.height = 7}
source(here::here("R", "02_heatmap.R"))
knitr::include_graphics(here("figures", "02_heatmap.png"))
```

Read this exactly like an expression heatmap: columns are samples (players),
rows are features (offensive rate stats), values are within-feature z-scores.
The dendrogram on the top axis is the same hierarchical clustering you'd run
on a cohort — players with similar offensive profiles end up adjacent.

## 3 · Volcano plot

```{r volcano, fig.width = 9, fig.height = 6}
source(here::here("R", "03_volcano.R"))
knitr::include_graphics(here("figures", "03_volcano.png"))
```

The x-axis is **effect size**: observed wOBA minus the Statcast expected
wOBA (`xwOBA`) derived from each player's batted-ball profile (exit
velocity, launch angle, sprint speed on grounders). The y-axis is the
**significance** of that gap given the player's plate appearances so far —
small samples sit near the floor; players who have separated from their
own expected line over a meaningful number of PAs get pushed up.

The cosmetic dashed gates are at ±0.020 wOBA and p < 0.05. Points outside
those gates are the season's "differentially expressed" hitters.

## 4 · PCA

```{r pca, fig.width = 9, fig.height = 6.5}
source(here::here("R", "04_pca.R"))
knitr::include_graphics(here("figures", "04_pca.png"))
```

Same biplot you'd produce from `prcomp()` on a count matrix: the player
scores cluster by offensive profile, and the feature loadings (the grey
arrows) tell you which stats are driving each axis. PC1 typically
separates power from on-base; PC2 picks up the strikeout/contact axis.

## 5 · Pitching staff as a sanity check

```{r pitching, fig.width = 9, fig.height = 5}
pitching |>
  dplyr::arrange(era) |>
  dplyr::mutate(player = forcats::fct_inorder(player)) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = player, y = era_minus_xera, fill = role)) +
  geom_col() +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, color = "grey40") +
  coord_flip() +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c(SP = "#0C2C56", RP = "#005C5C")) +
  labs(
    title    = "ERA − xERA: who is the bullpen getting away with it",
    x        = NULL,
    y        = "ERA − xERA  (negative = outperforming peripherals)",
    fill     = NULL
  )
```

## Takeaways for the demo

- **renv** pins the library; **Positron** is the IDE; **Coder** gives you
  the workspace. The notebook above does not care which machine renders it.
- Every plot here has a one-line analogue in a typical RNA-seq pipeline.
  Swap the matrix and the y-axis label and you have your own workflow.
- The fetch script's "live or synthetic" toggle is a generally useful
  pattern for teaching material that needs to work on a plane.
